loop.title: how a flag reaches the board
loop.description: Four cards in a row, joined left to right by arrows. Your agent runs the build, the build prints a line with a code in braces on it, you read that line, and you type what it says into the box on the board. A band under the first two cards says the machine is holding the work; a band under the last two says you are.
loop.agent.label: your agent
loop.build.label: the build
loop.you.label: you
loop.box.label: the board
flags.panel.title: Three runs, three flags
flags.panel.description: Everything on this board comes out of a build in kata/step0/java. Start your agent in there and work down the rows.
flags.panel.wrong: Not that one. Read the flag straight from the build output.
flag.run.label: The run
flag.run.hint: It is the block on the page before this one. Have your agent run it.
flag.run.help: This is the code block on the previous page, run for real. Open kata/step0/java, start your agent in there and ask it to run that block. There is nothing to work out: the build prints the flag on the line that says the intro is complete. Paste that code here, braces and all.
flag.ready.label: Ready to hunt
flag.ready.hint: Have your agent run mvn verify -Pready from the same folder.
flag.ready.help: It checks what the rest of the course assumes about your machine: the JDK Maven actually compiles with, and whether the other steps' projects are on disk. Pass both and the last row prints the flag. Fail one and the build names the check that failed and what to do about it, and prints no flag. The native-image row is a warning about step 2's last flag and never stops you.
flag.pick.label: Two candidates
flag.pick.hint: mvn verify -Ppick prints two strings in flag shape. Only one line is ticked.
flag.pick.help: Have your agent run mvn verify -Ppick and show you what came back rather than telling you what it said. Two lines return in the flag's exact shape and one of them carries a tick. An agent that read the run for you hands back both, or the wrong one, and sounds equally sure either way. Reading the tick is yours.
quiz.what-the-code-is.question: You are reading a page and hit a string in braces, like {f1r5t-5t3p5}. What is it doing there?
quiz.what-the-code-is.the-answer: It is the answer to a written exercise. You type it into the box to clear the page.
quiz.what-the-code-is.run-it: It is a snippet to run in your terminal, and its output is the real answer.
quiz.what-the-code-is.version: It is an internal id for the page, there for the authors and safe to skip.
quiz.what-the-code-is.placeholder: It is a placeholder that a tutor fills in during a guided session.
quiz.what-the-code-is.explanation: A string in braces is a flag, which means it is the answer itself. You clear the page by typing it back into the box, and it grades in your browser.
quiz.agent-says-it-found-it.question: You ask your agent for a flag. It comes back with a string in the right shape and says it is confident. It never ran anything. What have you got?
quiz.agent-says-it-found-it.a-guess: A guess. Have it run the thing and print the output, then read the flag off that.
quiz.agent-says-it-found-it.it-read-the-: A flag. It read the file, so the string came out of the code rather than out of the model.
quiz.agent-says-it-found-it.right-shape: A flag, as long as the shape is right. The shape is what the board checks your answer against.
quiz.agent-says-it-found-it.only-builds: Nothing usable. Only a build can print a flag, so a flag found by reading is never the right one.
quiz.agent-says-it-found-it.explanation: Worked out in prose, a flag is a plausible string with two letters wrong, said just as surely. The board hashes one exact string, so the cheapest check is to make the agent run the thing and read the answer out of the output.
